column2: The internal and external forces affecting business decisions
column3: A change in import duties can alter an Indian producer's costs even when its own management is unchanged.
column4: An external policy change cannot affect a business unless its management changes.

column2: Forces close to a firm such as suppliers and customers
column3: A supplier's refusal to extend credit changes the firm's immediate operating environment.
column4: A supplier's credit decision is a macroeconomic policy decision.

column2: Broad economic, political, legal and social forces
column3: An economy-wide inflation increase belongs to the general environment even when its effect differs between firms.
column4: An economy-wide inflation increase belongs only to the internal environment of affected firms.

column2: Systematic monitoring of relevant environmental changes
column3: Monitoring proposed regulations before launching a product can identify a threat before the regulation takes effect.
column4: Environmental scanning is useful only after a regulation has taken effect.

column2: The arrangement governing resource allocation and ownership
column3: An economy may combine private ownership with public provision of essential services.
column4: Private ownership in some sectors means the economy cannot have any public production.

column2: An economic system relying mainly on prices and private decisions
column3: When consumers buy more of a product, price signals can encourage producers to allocate resources toward it.
column4: In a market economy, a central authority must set every firm's output target.

column2: An economic system relying mainly on central planning
column3: A planning authority deciding sectoral output targets illustrates central allocation of resources.
column4: Central output targets necessarily illustrate allocation solely through competitive market prices.

column2: An economic system combining market mechanisms and government intervention
column3: Private firms and government enterprises can coexist without making the system purely centrally planned.
column4: The existence of any government enterprise makes all resource allocation centrally planned.

column2: Government decisions concerning public spending and taxation
column3: A higher government infrastructure budget, financed within the public budget, is a fiscal measure.
column4: A higher government infrastructure budget is a change in the central bank's policy interest rate.

column2: Central-bank measures influencing money, credit and interest rates
column3: A policy-rate increase can restrain credit demand, although transmission need not be immediate or complete.
column4: A policy-rate increase guarantees an immediate identical rise in every lending rate.

column2: A fiscal stance intended to support aggregate demand
column3: Other things equal, higher public expenditure can raise aggregate demand even when the central bank leaves its policy rate unchanged.
column4: Public expenditure can affect demand only if the central bank simultaneously lowers its policy rate.

column2: A monetary stance intended to restrain money or credit conditions
column3: Raising the policy rate can discourage borrowing; it does not directly enact a new income-tax rate.
column4: Raising the policy rate directly changes the statutory income-tax rate.

column2: Relaxation of government restrictions on economic activity
column3: Removing an industrial licensing requirement reduces an entry restriction without necessarily selling a public enterprise.
column4: Removing an industrial licensing requirement necessarily transfers a public enterprise to private ownership.

column2: Transfer of ownership or control from the public to the private sector
column3: A transfer of controlling government ownership to private investors illustrates privatisation.
column4: Allowing private firms to compete, without changing public ownership, necessarily privatises the public enterprise.

column2: Increasing integration of markets and economic activity across borders
column3: Lower communication and transport costs can help a firm coordinate production across countries.
column4: Globalisation requires the complete elimination of every national border and regulation.

column2: Social values, customs and demographic influences on business
column3: Different attitudes toward food consumption can require adaptation of the same restaurant brand's menu across countries.
column4: Identical branding guarantees identical consumer preferences in every country.

column2: Political institutions and government priorities affecting business
column3: A shift in government procurement priorities can change demand faced by suppliers.
column4: Government procurement priorities are entirely outside the political environment.

column2: Laws and regulatory obligations affecting business
column3: A business must distinguish consumer-protection obligations from a customer's voluntary preference.
column4: Consumer-protection obligations are merely optional preferences that firms may ignore.

column2: Business responsibility for social and environmental consequences
column3: A firm can examine effects on communities as well as shareholder returns when evaluating a project.
column4: Considering community effects necessarily means abandoning every financial objective.

column2: Considering groups affected by an organisation's actions
column3: Workers, customers and local communities may have legitimate interests even when they own no shares.
column4: Only registered shareholders can ever be stakeholders.

column2: India's legal framework for foreign-exchange management
column3: Under FEMA, distinguishing a current-account transaction from a capital-account transaction affects the applicable regulatory analysis.
column4: Under FEMA, every cross-border payment has the same regulatory classification regardless of its nature.

column2: The right to relevant and accurate product information
column3: Concealing a material product risk undermines informed consumer choice even when advertising is attractive.
column4: Attractive advertising removes the need to disclose material product risks.

column2: Selling domestically produced goods to buyers abroad
column3: A producer supplying goods abroad without owning a foreign factory can enter through exporting.
column4: Selling domestic output abroad always requires ownership of a foreign factory.

column2: Permission to use specified intellectual property for agreed consideration
column3: A foreign producer receiving permission to use a patent while operating independently illustrates licensing.
column4: A patent licence necessarily transfers ownership of the entire licensor company.

column2: Permission to use a business format and brand under an agreement
column3: A franchise can include operating standards and brand use while the outlet is owned by the franchisee.
column4: A franchise agreement necessarily makes every outlet a wholly owned subsidiary of the franchisor.

column2: A business undertaking owned jointly by participating parties
column3: Sharing ownership with a local partner can provide local knowledge while reducing unilateral control.
column4: Sharing ownership with a local partner gives the foreign investor complete unilateral control by definition.

column2: A subsidiary whose entire ownership belongs to its parent
column3: A parent owning all shares in a foreign subsidiary gains ownership control but still faces host-country law.
column4: Complete ownership exempts a foreign subsidiary from host-country law.

column2: Outsourcing production to another manufacturer under contract
column3: A firm may retain branding while another enterprise manufactures its products abroad.
column4: Outsourcing foreign production necessarily transfers ownership of the brand to the manufacturer.

column2: Producing a good with fewer resources than another producer
column3: If country A needs fewer labour hours for wheat than B, A has an absolute advantage in wheat in that labour-only model.
column4: Absolute advantage in wheat requires comparing wheat's opportunity cost rather than labour requirements.

column2: Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost
column3: A country can have comparative advantage in one good even if another country uses fewer labour hours for both goods.
column4: A country less productive in both goods can never benefit from specialisation under the comparative-cost model.

column2: Trade explained through relative factor endowments and factor intensities
column3: In the standard model, a relatively capital-abundant country tends to export relatively capital-intensive goods.
column4: The standard model predicts capital-abundant countries must export only labour-intensive goods.

column2: An import duty stated as a fixed amount per physical unit
column3: A duty of Rs 40 per imported unit is specific even when the invoice value changes.
column4: A duty of Rs 40 per unit is ad valorem because the total duty changes with quantity.

column2: An import duty calculated as a percentage of value
column3: At a 10% ad valorem duty, doubling the taxable import value doubles duty when the rate is unchanged.
column4: At a 10% ad valorem duty, the duty per consignment stays fixed regardless of value.

column2: A quantitative limit on imports
column3: A binding quantity cap can create scarcity rents; it does not automatically collect tariff revenue for the government.
column4: Every import quota automatically produces exactly the same government revenue as a tariff.

column2: A trade restriction other than a customs tariff
column3: An import licensing restriction may limit market access without changing the customs tariff rate.
column4: A restriction is a trade barrier only when it is explicitly a customs duty.

column2: Temporary protection to help an emerging industry develop
column3: The infant-industry case requires a reason why learning or development benefits cannot be adequately obtained without protection.
column4: Calling an industry new proves that permanent protection always raises national welfare.

column2: A trade remedy addressing qualifying dumped imports and injury
column3: A low foreign price alone is insufficient to establish every legal condition for an anti-dumping duty.
column4: Every imported product cheaper than a domestic product automatically qualifies for anti-dumping duty.

column2: Cross-border investment establishing a lasting interest with significant influence
column3: An investment giving lasting influence over a foreign enterprise differs from merely holding tradable securities for portfolio returns.
column4: Every foreign securities purchase is automatically direct investment regardless of influence.

column2: Cross-border investment in financial assets without direct managerial control
column3: A diversified foreign share portfolio can seek financial returns without establishing managerial control.
column4: Portfolio investment requires the investor to manage the issuer's daily operations.

column2: Creating a new operating facility through investment
column3: Constructing a new factory abroad is greenfield entry rather than purchasing an already operating factory.
column4: Buying an existing operating factory is greenfield investment merely because the buyer is foreign.

column2: Investment involving an existing facility or business
column3: Acquiring an existing foreign production facility avoids starting every physical asset from scratch.
column4: Acquiring an existing facility always means constructing an entirely new site.

column2: Foreign direct investment in similar business activities
column3: A manufacturer producing the same product in a foreign plant illustrates horizontal rather than upstream vertical FDI.
column4: Producing the same product abroad is upstream vertical FDI simply because production is overseas.

column2: Foreign direct investment in a different stage of a value chain
column3: A car producer acquiring a foreign component supplier illustrates backward vertical integration.
column4: A car producer acquiring its component supplier illustrates forward integration toward final consumers.

column2: The BOP account recording goods, services and primary and secondary income
column3: Payment for an imported service is recorded in the current account rather than as acquisition of an equity asset.
column4: All foreign payments belong to the financial account because money changes hands.

column2: The BOP account recording transactions in financial assets and liabilities
column3: A foreign direct equity investment is a financial-account transaction under the BPM6 classification.
column4: A foreign direct equity investment is a goods export in the current account.

column2: The difference between merchandise exports and merchandise imports
column3: A merchandise trade deficit can coexist with a smaller current-account deficit when net service receipts are positive.
column4: A merchandise trade deficit necessarily equals the current-account deficit regardless of services and income.

column2: Integration removing internal trade barriers while members retain their external tariffs
column3: Members may maintain different tariffs toward non-members, making rules of origin relevant.
column4: A free trade area necessarily requires a single common external tariff.

column2: Integration combining internal free trade with a common external tariff
column3: Removing internal tariffs and adopting a common external tariff goes beyond a free trade area.
column4: A customs union by definition guarantees unrestricted factor mobility and a single currency.

column2: Replacement of higher-cost domestic production by lower-cost partner imports
column3: Switching from costly domestic output to cheaper partner output can improve resource allocation.
column4: Replacing a cheaper non-member supplier with a costlier partner is trade creation.

column2: Replacement of lower-cost non-member imports by higher-cost partner imports
column3: A tariff preference can redirect purchases to a costlier partner even when the partner is not the lowest-cost producer.
column4: Every increase in trade with a partner proves that the lowest-cost world supplier has been selected.

column2: A customs union with freer movement of factors of production
column3: Factor mobility can be added to internal free trade and a common external tariff without necessarily adopting one currency.
column4: A common market necessarily has a single currency and a single fiscal authority.

column2: The institution associated with monetary cooperation and balance-of-payments support
column3: A balance-of-payments financing problem falls within the IMF's core mandate rather than making it a world trade court.
column4: The IMF's core mandate is adjudicating every dispute over WTO tariff concessions.

column2: The institution associated with development finance
column3: Financing a long-term development project aligns with the World Bank's development role.
column4: The World Bank's principal role is setting every member country's policy interest rate.

column2: The UN body concerned with trade and development
column3: UNCTAD's trade-and-development work differs from the WTO's rules and dispute framework.
column4: UNCTAD and the WTO are the same organisation with identical enforcement powers.

column2: The organisation administering multilateral trade agreements
column3: WTO commitments constrain trade policy but do not imply that all tariffs must be zero.
column4: WTO membership prohibits every tariff without exception.

column2: The WTO agreement dealing with trade in services
column3: A service supplied by establishing a foreign commercial presence belongs to a GATS supply mode.
column4: GATS covers only physically shipped manufactured goods.

column2: The WTO agreement on trade-related intellectual property rights
column3: Trade-related patent obligations fall under TRIPS rather than TRIMS.
column4: TRIPS principally regulates local-content requirements imposed on investors.

column2: The WTO agreement on trade-related investment measures
column3: A local-content requirement linked to investment can raise TRIMS issues rather than being an intellectual-property rule.
column4: TRIMS is the WTO agreement governing patent duration and copyright protection.

column2: The WTO agreement concerning agricultural trade disciplines
column3: Market access, domestic support and export competition are distinct areas of agricultural trade disciplines.
column4: The Agreement on Agriculture has no concern with domestic support measures.

column2: Preferential integration arrangements between participating economies
column3: EU, ASEAN, SAARC and the historical NAFTA represent different regional arrangements with different depths of integration.
column4: All regional trade arrangements require the same currency and the same degree of factor mobility.
